53	                                      Locked Bag 1797
54	                                      Penrith, NSW 2751, Australia
55	                                      Phone: +61 (0)2 4620 3304
56	                                      Email: R.Lovell@westernsyndey.edu.au
57	
58	             This article has been accepted for publication and undergone full peer review but has not
59	             been through the copyediting, typesetting, pagination and proofreading process, which may
60	             lead to differences between this version and the Version of Record. Please cite this article as
61	             doi: 10.1111/sms.13226
62	             This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.
63	               Running Head: Scheduling Injury Prevention in Soccer
64	
65	
66	
67	
68	Accepted Article
69	             Scheduling of Eccentric Lower-limb Injury Prevention Exercises during the Soccer
70	             micro-cycle: Which day of the week?
71	
72	
73	
74	             Abstract
75	
76	             Scheduling eccentric-based injury prevention programs (IPP) during the common 6-day
77	             micro-cycle in Soccer is challenged by recovery and tapering phases. This study profiled
78	             muscle damage, neuromuscular performance, and perceptual responses to a lower-limb
79	             eccentric-based IPP administered 1 (MD+1) versus 3 days (MD+3) post-match. 18 semi-
80	             professional players were monitored daily during 3 in-season 6-day micro-cycles, including
81	             weekly competitive fixtures. Capillary creatine kinase concentration (CK), posterior lower
82	             limb isometric peak force (PF), counter-movement jump (CMJ) performance, and muscle
83	             soreness were assessed 24 h prior to match-day (baseline), and every 24 h up to 120 h
84	             post-match. The IPP consisted of lunges, single stiff leg dead-lifts, single leg-squats and
85	             Nordic hamstring exercises. Performing the IPP on MD+1 attenuated the decline in CK
86	             normally observed following match-play           (CON: 142%; MD+3: 166%; small
87	             differences). When IPP was delivered on MD+3, CK was higher versus CON and MD+1
88	             trials on both MD+4 (MD+3: 260%; CON: 146%; MD+1: 151%; moderate differences) and
89	             MD+5 (MD+3: 209%; CON: 125%; MD+1: 127%; small differences). Soreness ratings were
90	             not exacerbated when the IPP was delivered on MD+1, but when prescribed on MD+3,
91	             hamstring soreness ratings remained higher on MD+4 and MD+5 (small differences). No
92	             between trial differences were observed for PF and CMJ. Administering the IPP in the
93	             middle of the micro-cycle (MD+3) increased measures of muscle damage and soreness,
94	             which remained elevated on the day prior to the next match (MD+5). Accordingly, IPP
95	             should be scheduled early in the micro-cycle, to avoid compromising preparation for the
96	             following match.
97	
98	
99	
100	             Keywords: injury prevention, scheduling, muscle, soccer
101	
102	
103	
104	             Introduction
105	
106	             Soccer has a problem with injuries. Injury rates in both professional 1-3 and amateur soccer
107	             (9.6 injuries/1000h 1) exceed those observed both in industrial occupational settings 4 and
108	             other outdoor sports 5. The economic burden of injuries is substantial 6, and has also been
109	             shown to transcend to soccer performance outcomes, where teams with more injuries have
110	             been less successful on the pitch 7,8. Whilst some soccer injuries are inevitable (i.e. trauma
111	             injuries), 58% of injuries occur without contact and are considered preventable 3. The most
112	             common injury type are muscle strain injuries (31-37%), predominantly occurring in the
113	             hamstrings, adductors, quadriceps and calves 1-3. Although injury prevention programs (IPP)
114	             are commonplace in high-level professional soccer teams, there is a lack of information
115	
116	
117	
118	
119	             This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.
120	              about how to schedule these sessions in the context of a training week during the
121	             competitive season 9.
122	
123	
124	
125	
126	Accepted Article
127	             A survey of 44 ‘Premier League’ teams from around the world identified that the adoption of
128	             IPP was ubiquitous, with an average of 5.1 ± 2.4 practitioners (doctors, physiotherapists,
129	             sport scientists) employed to administer the programs 9. Eccentric exercises were ranked
130	             the most effective modality implemented within IPP 9. The theoretical basis for the inclusion
131	             of eccentric strengthening exercises include the greater mechanical tension and strain
132	             exerted upon the muscle fibers 10, yielding increases in muscle fascicle length 11,12 that
133	             consequently increase muscle shortening velocity and force production at longer muscle
134	             lengths 10,12. Whilst IPP consisting of eccentric exercises are warranted on the basis of the
135	             enhanced muscle function and architectural adaptations, the residual muscle fatigue and
136	             damage incurred 13 presents a scheduling dilemma for injury prevention specialists. This
137	             challenge is exacerbated in soccer, where competition schedules mandate a delicate
138	             balance between providing adequate recovery from competition and training, in combination
139	             with a suitable maintenance stimulus to prevent declines in muscle strength and lower limb
140	             power that have been documented over the course of a season 14-16.
141	
142	
143	
144	             According to the available literature, intense soccer training is not scheduled in the 24-48 h
145	             period post-match 17-19, to facilitate recovery of muscle function and damage. In micro-
146	             cycles consisting of one competitive match per week, the greatest volume of on-field training
147	             is typically scheduled in the middle of the training week, between 2-4 days prior to the match
148	             19,20
149	                  , with IPP most commonly delivered 48-72 h post-match 9. However, considering the
150	             muscle damage and residual fatigue inflicted from eccentric exercise may persist for 48-72
151	             hours 21-23, current IPP scheduling in the middle of the training week may impact upon
152	             subsequent physical match performance. Moreover, during congested fixture periods (2 or
153	             more matches per week) common to soccer, IPP are often sacrificed to prepare for, or
154	             compete in, the following match 9, which over-time may result in muscle de-training 14,15,24
155	             and render the player more susceptible to injury 25. To our knowledge, a dearth of evidence
156	             is available regarding the scheduling and subsequent recovery from an IPP session in
157	             relation to soccer matches 9.
158	
159	
160	
161	             The purpose of this study was to examine the acute impact of scheduling an eccentric-based
162	             lower-limb IPP on different days of the micro-cycle upon muscle function, damage, and
163	             soreness. Assessment of these muscle responses can inform the scheduling of IPP in
164	             soccer micro-cycles, and provide relevant insight to practitioners dealing with congested
165	             fixtures.
166	
167	
168	
169	
170	             This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.
171	              Materials and methods
172	
173	             Participants
174	
175	
176	
177	
178	Accepted Article
179	             Eighteen semi-professional outfield players (Age: 22.9 ± 4.5; Stature: 178.4 ± 8.7 cm; Body
180	             Mass: 74.5 ± 11.3 kg) were recruited from three teams competing in the 3rd and 4th tiers of
181	             the Australian Soccer pyramid during the 2015 season. These players typically undertake 2
182	             field-based training sessions, perform in one or two competitive fixtures, and 1-3 gymnasium
183	             conditioning sessions (on an independent, self-selected basis) per in-season week. The
184	             study obtained ethical approval from the Western Sydney University human research
185	             committee, and each player provided written informed consent to participate.
186	
187	
188	
189	             Experimental Design
190	
191	             Within a cross-over design, players were randomized into three groups within each team
192	             (n=6) to ensure that the order of experimental trials could be counter-balanced and limit the
193	             impact of extraneous factors such as weather conditions, training and competition loads etc.
194	             Allocation was performed using a spreadsheet to reduce between group differences in
195	             controlled trials (Hopkins, 2010), using participant characteristics in the following priority
196	             order: team, peak posterior limb isometric force (see details below), positional role, age and
197	             body mass. Table 1 displays the characteristics of players in each group
198	
199	
200	
201	             Over a 3-week period, players undertook three experimental conditions in 6-day micro-
202	             cycles. The micro-cycles were selected on the basis that only one match was scheduled on
203	             weekends, and there were no expected changes to the routine training program that
204	             included two soccer training sessions each week. The 6-day micro-cycles commenced on
205	             match-day (MD), and outcome measures were tracked for the following 5-days, which
206	             included on-field training sessions scheduled 3 (MD+3) and 5 days (MD+5) post MD. During
207	             each micro-cycle, players training and match training loads were determined; and subjective,
208	             biochemical and performance recovery profiles were assessed 24 h prior to match-day
209	             (baseline), and 24 (MD+1), 48 (MD+2), 72 (MD+3), 96 (MD+4) and 120 h (MD+5) post-
210	             match.
211	
212	
213	
214	             The experimental design included a control micro-cycle (CON), in which the players training
215	             loads and recovery parameters were monitored without any intervention. The impact of
216	             scheduling was examined using two treatment trials in which an eccentric-based IPP
217	             focusing on the anterior and posterior thigh muscles was administered either ~24- (MD+ 1)
218	             or ~72-h (MD+3) post-match, immediately following the recordings of muscle performance,
219	             damage and recovery measures. We selected the scheduling in our two treatment trials
220	             based on the survey of McCall and colleagues 9, which demonstrated that whilst the majority
221	             (61%) of teams prescribed IPP between 48-72 h post-match, a notable proportion (16%)
222	             delivered an IPP within 24 h of the match, highlighting the uncertainty in professional
223	             practice.
224	
225	
226	
227	
228	             This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.
229	              The IPP was based on a program administered to elite level soccer players in a premier
230	             level European club, and consisted of 4 exercises depicted in figure 1; lunges, single stiff-
231	             legged deadlift with 6 kg kettle-bell, single leg eccentric squats (all 4 x 5 repetitions on each
232	
233	
234	
235	
236	Accepted Article
237	             limb) and Nordic hamstring exercises (NHE) performed on a Bosu-ball (4 x 5 repetitions).
238	             The Bosu-ball was used for the NHE to accentuate the eccentric stimulus at extended
239	             muscle lengths, the joint position which corresponds with the mechanism of hamstring injury
240	             26
241	                and positioning in which the greatest NHE-induced strength gains are observed 12. These
242	             exercises were selected because injuries to the hamstring and quadriceps are amongst the
243	             most prevalent in soccer 1-3, and that eccentric exercises are considered the most important
244	             feature of IPP by soccer specialists 9. The IPP was performed under direct supervision of
245	             both a chartered physiotherapist (MW) and a sport scientist (RL) to ensure appropriate and
246	             consistent exercise techniques. Players had been familiarized with the IPP program
247	             following two training sessions in the 2-weeks preceding the study.
248	
249	
250	
251	             Outcome Measures
252	
253	             On the day prior to the match, and each day of the micro-cycle (excluding match-day),
254	             players attended a training ground to perform the battery of measures. Upon arrival, players
255	             warmed-up by running around a marked area on the training pitch for 5-minutes at 10 km/h
256	             (running speed standardized via a metronome). Upon completion, a capillary blood sample
257	             was drawn to determine plasma creatine kinase, which was used as an indirect estimate of
258	             muscle damage 27. Next, players were fitted with a knee brace to undertake the assessment
259	             of posterior lower-limb isometric peak force. During a subsequent 4-min rest interval players
260	             recorded their subjective evaluations of any training load incurred over the previous 24
261	             hours, and ratings of perceived muscle soreness. Finally, players performed the maximal
262	             counter-movement jump assessments. Players were familiarized with the outcome measure
263	             procedures on two occasions prior to data collection.
264	
265	
266	
267	             Creatine Kinase
268	
269	             Duplicate capillary blood samples were drawn from the fingertip and collected in heparinzed
270	             capillary tubes. 30 μl samples were immediately transferred onto reagent strips and the
271	             concentration of creatine kinase in the plasma was measured via Reflectance photometry
272	             (Reflotron IV, Boehringer Mannheim, Germany). The spectrometer was calibrated prior to
273	             each day using manufacturer supplied calibration strips. Where duplicate samples were
274	             either dubious or markedly different, additional samples were collected. The mean of two
275	             acceptable CK recordings was used for subsequent analysis (3.5% coefficient of variation;
276	             measurement range: 24.4-1400 UL-1).
277	
278	
279	
280	             Isometric Muscle Strength
281	
282	             Posterior lower limb isometric peak force was measured on the dominant limb at 30° of knee
283	             flexion (0° = full knee extension) according to the methods adopted in previous soccer
284	             studies 21,28. We adopted an isometric modality that is sensitive to neuromuscular fatigue
285	
286	
287	
288	
289	             This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.
290	              induced by soccer match-play 21,28, and deemed feasible for daily monitoring to limit the
291	             impact of the maximum contractions upon the time-course of muscle function recovery.
292	             Knee flexion angle was sustained throughout the contraction using a knee brace that was
293	
294	
295	
296	
297	Accepted Article
298	             fixed according to an inherent goniometer (Orthopaedic Appliances Pty Ltd, Australia). The
299	             heel of the dominant leg was placed on a 1000hz piezoelectric force platform (Kistler
300	             Instruments Pty Ltd, Australia) wired to a data acquisition system and attached to a plinth,
301	             with the non-dominant leg fully extended below the plinth (See Figure 2). Players were
302	             instructed to push their dominant heel into the force platform “as fast and as forcefully as
303	             possible” during three maximal 3 s contractions, separated by a 2-min rest period. Force
304	             data was smoothed with a sliding 200 ms window and the peak force (N) was recorded for
305	             analysis, having corrected for passive limb-mass. The typical error (expressed as a
306	             percentage co-efficient of variation) established from the three baseline (MD-1) recordings of
307	             isometric peak force was 8.2 % (90% confidence intervals [CI]: 6.7 to 11.2%).
308	
309	
310	
311	             Counter-movement Jump
312	
313	             The counter-movement jump is a commonly used tool to track neuromuscular recovery
314	             following soccer match-play 21,29. Players performed two maximal counter-movement jumps
315	             (CMJ; hands placed on hips for the duration of the attempt), interceded by 2 minutes of
316	             passive recovery. The speed and depth of the countermovement phase were self-selected.
317	             Players performed the CMJ on a force platform (Precision Calibration Systems, Sydney,
318	             Australia), with force signal sampled at 1000Hz. The analogue to digital converter signal
319	             was calibrated prior to each day using a known mass, and the signal was zeroed in between
320	             each participant to avoid drift. The vertical force trace was collected (Powerlab 16/35, ADI
321	             instruments, Australia; 16-bit analogue to digital conversion) and smoothed by a digital low
322	             pass filter cut off at 50 Hz. The flight-time:contraction-time ratio was recorded according to
323	             previously outlined procedures 30, and the jump height (cm) estimated from time in flight 31.
324	             The baseline coefficients of variation for CMJ height and flight-time:contraction-time ratio
325	             were 5.8% (CI: 4.8-7.9%) and 9.5% (CI: 7.7-12.7%), respectively.
326	
327	
328	
329	             Perceived Muscle Soreness
330	
331	             Daily ratings of perceived soreness in the hamstring and quadricep muscle groups were
332	             reported at rest. Players used a 100 mm visual analogue scale superimposed with the
333	             following verbal anchors: 0 = “absolutely no soreness”, and 100 = “the most muscle
334	             soreness that they could possibly bear” 32.
335	
336	
337	
338	
339	             This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.
340	              Monitoring Variables
341	
342	             External Load
343	
344	
345	
346	
347	Accepted Article
348	             During matches, players wore a 10Hz GPS device (MinimaX S4, Catapult, Australia) affixed
349	             in a neoprene under-garment worn beneath their training/playing jersey. Players wore the
350	             same device and undergarment throughout the study to attenuate within-subject error.
351	             Doppler velocity data was pre-processed using the manufacturers ‘Intelligent Motion Filter’
352	             and the minimum effort duration was set at 0.2 secs (Catapult Sprint, version 5.1.7, Catapult
353	             Sports, Australia). GPS data were extracted and further processed using R (version 3.01).
354	             Instantaneous observations of velocity and acceleration were discarded when the number of
355	             satellites informing the receiver was less than 6, and/or the horizontal dilution of precision
356	             (HDOP) was less than 1.25. The average proportion of data discarded during match files
357	             was 0.19 ± 0.21% of total playing time. All match observations therefore met the inclusion
358	             criteria, whereby extracted instantaneous data accounted for <3% of the total session
359	             duration. Players’ total distance covered (TDC) and that covered at high- (HSR; > 15.0 kmh-
360	             1
361	              ) and sprinting (SPR; > 23.0 kmh-1) running speeds were computed for each session.
362	
363	
364	
365	             Internal Load
366	
367	             The internal load was calculated using the session-RPE method 33, recorded 10 minutes
368	             after all training and matches during each micro-cycle. Players were also asked to
369	             retrospectively rate exertion and provide training duration(s) for any additional conditioning
370	             sessions performed outside of the team environment. These ratings were collected on a
371	             daily basis during the recovery profiling assessments for the previous 24-hour period.
372	             Recent observations suggest that sessional RPE ratings are robust measures even when
373	             collected retrospectively 34.
374	
375	
376	
377	             Statistics
378	
379	             For statistical analysis, outcome measures were expressed as change scores from the
380	             relevant micro-cycle baseline measure, and subsequently log-transformed to reduce non-
381	             uniformity error. Linear mixed models (IBM SPSS version 23.0, Armonk, NY) were used to
382	             examine the impact of scheduling upon the recovery time-course of muscle function,
383	             soreness and damage markers. The experimental trial and measurement day were entered
384	             into the model as fixed factors, and within-player variance was modeled as a random factor.
385	             In addition, sRPE and baseline measures of the relevant dependent variable were imputed
386	             as covariates in the model. Baseline recordings accounted for week-to-week changes, and
387	             sRPE adjusted for variations in internal training load both within and between micro-cycles
388	             for each individual player. P-values generated from least-squared difference post hoc tests,
389	             in combination with back-transformed estimated marginal mean effect statistics, were
390	             imputed into a spreadsheet 35 to derive magnitude-based inferences. The magnitude of the
391	             effect was classified as small, moderate, or large according to standardized fractions (0.2,
392	             0.6, and 1.2) of the pooled between-subject standard deviation, calculated from measures
393	             collected 24 h post-match (MD+1) in the each trial. We elected to use MD+1 data to anchor
394	             standardized thresholds considering the large between-subject variation in responses to
395	
396	
397	
398	             This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.
399	              soccer match-play, and to avoid type II error. Inferences were determined from the
400	             disposition of the 90% confidence interval for the mean difference in reference to the
401	             standardized thresholds (likely = >75%; very-likely = > 95%; most-likely > 99.5%), but
402	
403	
404	
405	
406	Accepted Article
407	             regarded as unclear if the confidence intervals overlapped both positive and negative
408	             thresholds by 5% 36. Data are reported as the back-transformed estimated marginal means
409	             (adjusted for sRPE and relevant baseline measures) with corresponding 90% intervals.
410	
411	
412	
413	             Results
414	
415	             Compliance
416	
417	             17 players undertook all 3 micro-cycles and fully complied to the IPP. One player completed
418	             one micro-cycle, before withdrawing due to a contact injury sustained during a match.
419	
420	
421	
422	             Match Loads
423	
424	             Table 2 presents external and internal load data collected during the three competitive
425	             matches, according to the experimental trial. Match-day external load measures (TDC,
426	             HSR) were likely lower in the MD + 3 trial (small-moderate effects), however no internal load
427	             (sRPE) differences were identified between experimental conditions. The matches were
428	             also played in similar ambient temperature (CON: 18.3 + 1.5; MD+1: 18.5 + 2.4; MD+3: 19.2
429	             + 2.9) and relative humidity (CON: 44.1 + 18.8%; MD+1: 42.3 + 18.0%; MD+3: 39.6 +
430	             17.1%).
431	
432	
433	
434	             Muscle Damage
435	
436	             Creatine Kinase responses to the study can be observed in Figure 3. CK was 256% (CI:
437	             225-292%) of baseline 24 hours post-match, with no between trial differences observed.
438	             Expressed as percentage change from baseline, performing the IPP 24 h after the match
439	             (MD+1) attenuated the decline in CK (197%; CI: 166-233%) at MD+2 (likely small effects)
440	             versus CON (142%; CI: 120-170%) and MD+3 (166%; CI: 140-196%). Administering the
441	             IPP 72 h following the match (MD+3) increased CK versus CON and MD+1 on both MD+4
442	             (MD+3: 260%; CI: 219-310%; CON: 146%; CI: 121-176%; MD+1: 151%; CI: 127-180%;
443	             likely moderate effects) and MD+5 (MD+3: 209%; CI: 176-248%; CON: 125%; CI: 105 to
444	             150%; MD+1: 127%; CI: 106 to 151%; likely to very-likely small effects).
445	
446	
447	
448	             Muscle Soreness
449	
450	             Soreness ratings (VAS 0-100) of the hamstring and quadricep muscle groups are presented
451	             in panes A and B, respectively, of Figure 4. Hamstring soreness increased 4.8-fold following
452	             match play, with no between trial differences, and returned to baseline after 72 hours in
453	             CON. Hamstring soreness following the match was not exacerbated by undertaking the IPP
454	             on the following day (MD+1), as observed over the subsequent 72 hours. Alternatively,
455	             when the IPP was administered on MD+3, hamstring soreness remained higher on MD+4
456	
457	
458	
459	             This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.
460	              (26.9; CI: 20.3-33.4 AU) and MD+5 (22.5; CI: 16.2-28.9 AU) versus CON (MD+4: 7.0; CI:
461	             0.2-13.7 AU; MD+5: 9.5; CI: 3.1-16.0 AU) and MD+1 trials (MD+4: 8.2; CI: 1.9-14.6 AU;
462	             MD+5: 7.1; CI: 0.8-13.4 AU; likely to very-likely small effects).
463	
464	
465	
466	
467	Accepted Article
468	             Quadriceps soreness also increased (+16.2; 90%CI: 11.8-20.5 AU) 24 h post matches, and
469	             returned to baseline by MD+3 irrespective of the trial. Scheduling of the IPP on either MD+1
470	             or MD+3 had no effect upon quadriceps soreness across the micro-cycle.
471	
472	
473	
474	             Performance Measures
475	
476	             Changes in performance measures according to both the micro-cycle and experimental trial
477	             are presented in Figure 4. Posterior lower limb strength (panel A) was lower at baseline in
478	             CON versus MD+3 (likely small difference), however no other between trial differences were
479	             observed during the micro-cycle when adjusted for both baseline data and sRPE. Posterior
480	             lower-limb strength also did not change across the micro-cycle, irrespective of the
481	             experimental trial.
482	
483	
484	
485	             Flight time:contraction time ratio (panel B) did not differ either across the micro-cycle or
486	             between experimental trials. CMJ height was 3.7% lower versus baseline at 24 h post-
487	             match (likely small effect; panel C), and performance returned to baseline on MD+2. There
488	             were no differences between the experimental trials in CMJ performance.
489	
490	
491	
492	             Discussion
493	
494	             In this study we examined the impact of IPP scheduling within 6-day micro-cycles upon
495	             muscle function, soreness, and creatine kinase as an indirect measure of damage.
496	             Administering the eccentric-based IPP 24 hours following matches slowed the rate of
497	             creatine kinase decay, but did not exacerbate soreness beyond the typical recovery time-
498	             course. In contrast, delivering the IPP in the middle of the micro-cycle (MD+3) increased
499	             measures of soreness and damage, which remained elevated on the day prior to the
500	             following match (MD+5). IPP scheduling had no impact upon the muscle function measures
501	             adopted in this study. To our knowledge, this is the first study to examine the impact of IPP
502	             scheduling during a typical micro-cycle in soccer, and our preliminary findings infer that
503	             administering eccentric-based exercises in the middle of the training week may negatively
504	             impact upon preparation for the following match. Moreover, delivery early in the micro-cycle
505	             ensures that the training stimulus is not sacrificed during congested fixtures periods in which
506	             matches are played every 3-4 days.
507	
508	
509	
510	             Surveys of current industry practice suggest that IPP are commonly scheduled 48-72 hours
511	             following a match, and that eccentric-based exercises are considered the most effective
512	             modality 9. When we administered an eccentric-based IPP 72 hours following match-play
513	
514	
515	
516	
517	             This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.
518	              (MD+3), robust CK and hamstring muscle soreness responses were observed (Figures 3
519	             and 4), and remained elevated 24 h prior to the next match in 6-day micro-cycles. Although
520	             acute muscle function was not impaired following the eccentric IPP in this study (Figure 5),
521	
522	
523	
524	
525	Accepted Article
526	             higher residual values of CK prior to team-sport training and competitive matches have been
527	             associated with reduced explosive running 37 and technical performance ratings 38.
528	             Whereas, self-reported muscle soreness collected pre-training or pre-match have a trivial
529	             association with external load parameters 39,40, and to the authors knowledge there is no
530	             published literature evaluating the impact of soreness ratings on subsequent non-contact
531	             injury risk. Notwithstanding, collectively these observations would suggest that scheduling
532	             IPP in the middle of the micro-cycle may compromise performance in the following match,
533	             however further work may be necessary to confirm whether repeated high-intensity actions
534	             that better reflect the nature of soccer activity are unhindered following eccentric IPP.
535	
536	
537	
538	             Although training load studies have implied that the greatest volume of both on-field 19,20 and
539	             IPP training 9 is performed in the middle of the micro-cycle, following approximately 24-48 h
540	             post-match recovery 17-19, 7 of the 44 teams surveyed by McCall and colleagues 9 reported
541	             delivering an IPP within 24 h post-match. When IPP was scheduled on MD+1 in the current
542	             study, CK decay was slowed 48 h post-match, but returned to baseline after 72 h, and the
543	             time-course of muscle function and soreness recovery post-match was not affected. These
544	             observations to some degree are supported by previous work, which showed that
545	             prescribing an upper-body strength training session 24 h following a bout of damaging lower-
546	             limb eccentric actions 13 did not adversely impact recovery kinetics (hamstring strength, CK,
547	             muscle soreness).        Whilst training structures in micro-cycles consisting of weekly
548	             competition schedules typically comprise of recovery and regenerative strategies, the
549	             inclusion of additional training 24 h post-match may optimize the limited time available for
550	             training, and offset the seasonal losses in strength and power in team-sports 14-16. Whilst a
551	             potentially attractive solution to training prescription in congested competition schedules,
552	             further work is necessary to determine both the acute and chronic responses to
553	             administering an IPP during the typical muscle regenerative phase of the weekly soccer
554	             micro-cycle in which muscle function may be compromised.
555	
556	
557	
558	             The increase in creatine kinase observed 24 h post match in this study (256% vs. 98-300%),
559	             together with the decay recorded at 48 (142% vs. 45-300%) and 72 h (138% vs. 90-202%) in
560	             the control trial, was comparable to previous research 21-23,41. Furthermore, the response
561	             magnitudes for soreness recorded in our control trial far exceeded those reported previously
562	             in elite cohorts 21,22,42 at 24 and 48 h post-match. Despite the robust CK and soreness
563	             responses observed, the muscle function measures adopted in our study were generally not
564	             sensitive to soccer match-play. Only peak counter-movement jump height was reduced 24
565	             hours post-match, with no change documented in FT:CT ratio, or the isometric assessment
566	             of posterior lower-limb peak force. Our data on lower-limb power and strength are in
567	             contrast with other work documenting the recovery time-course of neuromuscular function
568	             following team-sports match play 21,29. Given the equivalent internal responses to soccer
569	             match-play we observed when contrasting to previous work, it is difficult to reconcile this
570	             disparity. However, because we were not able to influence team selection in our study,
571	             players were at times selected as substitutes or were early withdrawals from the game,
572	
573	
574	
575	             This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.
576	              which to an extent reflects the low external loads reported herein. Accordingly, the
577	             impairment of neuromuscular function likely had a high degree of variability in our study,
578	             which may explain the lack of differences observed.
579	
580	
581	
582	
583	Accepted Article
584	             Of note was that the IPP induced the same acute CK magnitude response versus match-
585	             play, when delivered on MD+3. This was surprising considering that the players were
586	             familiar with the IPP, but may reflect the lower training status of our semi-professional
587	             cohort. For example, the mean baseline isometric peak strength recorded in this study was
588	             ~20-30% lower than that reported for the same procedure in professional players 21,28. It is
589	             also noteworthy that individuals with a strength training history recover muscle function and
590	             CK responses back to baseline quicker than their untrained counterparts 43. It may be the
591	             case that professional players routinely exposed to eccentric muscle actions during both IPP
592	             and soccer activity have a blunted response and faster CK decay following IPP. This may
593	             be due to structural reinforcement of muscle fibers, or the addition of sarcomeres in series
594	             which renders the fascicles more resistant to stretch, potentially reducing mechanical
595	             disruption and microscopic trauma 44. The semi-professional cohort examined in this study
596	             had a mixed strength-training history, but were familiar with lower-limb eccentric exercises,
597	             and were exposed to the eccentric nature of soccer activity between 3-4 times per week,
598	             with a particularly rigorous soreness and CK response to matches. Hence, whilst
599	             generalization of the current findings to professional programs is speculative, we would
600	             caution against administering eccentric-based IPP in the middle of the micro-cycle in
601	             professional team-sports.
602	
603	
604	
605	             The major limiting factor of the current study was the administration of a standardized IPP
606	             that did not take into consideration the differing training histories and capacities of the
607	             individual players. We recognize that in applied practice athletes may undertake tailored
608	             IPP, but we considered standardization necessary given the cross-over design adopted, and
609	             the challenges in prescribing individualized eccentric training intensity and volume. In
610	             contrast, we were unable to standardize the match stimulus given our preference for an
611	             ecologically natured study, and with the exception of load monitoring could not access the
612	             players on match-day to ascertain measures of muscle function, damage and soreness
613	             immediately pre- and post matches. An examination of physical match performance
614	             following the IPP delivery at MD+1 or MD+3 may have provided further insight on the impact
615	             of IPP scheduling, however we omitted this analysis considering the high-degree of
616	             between-match variation in high-speed running and sprinting 45. Interpretation of CK derived
617	             from blood samples as an indicator of muscle damage is confounded by its unknown origin,
618	             and can often be explained by blunt force traumas in sporting settings where collisions are
619	             commonplace 46. Finally, generalizability of the current findings should be tempered
620	             considering the semi-professional cohort adopted, whose training history, micro-cycle
621	             schedules, and capacity may influence the acute muscle responses following the eccentric-
622	             IPP, and may not directly translate into professional practice.
623	
624	
625	
626	
627	             This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.
628	              In summary, scheduling an eccentric-based injury prevention program in the middle of a 6-
629	             day micro-cycle left residual impairments in muscle soreness and damage on the day prior
630	             to the next match. Alternatively, administering the program 24 hours post-match had limited
631	
632	
633	
634	
635	Accepted Article
636	             impact on recovery kinetics. The results would suggest that delivering eccentric injury
637	             prevention exercises earlier in the micro-cycle does not impact on subsequent match
638	             preparation, and that this strategy may avoid in-season detraining which renders the player
639	             more susceptible to injury, particularly considering that IPP are often sacrificed during
640	             congested fixture schedules involving 2 or 3 matches per week.
641	
642	
643	
644	             Perspectives
645	
646	             The incidence and location of injuries in Soccer is well established 1-3, and substantial
647	             resources have been allocated to injury prevention 9. However, scheduling of eccentric-
648	             based injury prevention programs is challenged by fixture congestion, and the inherent need
649	             to recover from, and prepare for, competitive matches. The insights from this study provide
650	             some preliminary evidence to guide sports medicine professional practice, however further
651	             work is warranted considering the multitude of factors governing the scheduling of injury
652	             prevention programs. Further knowledge generation in the area of injury prevention
653	             scheduling will assist both Soccer teams and their governing associations in reducing the
654	             high burden of injury, and may inform fixture-scheduling policy.
655

               Running Head: Scheduling Injury Prevention in Soccer




Accepted Article
             Scheduling of Eccentric Lower-limb Injury Prevention Exercises during the Soccer
             micro-cycle: Which day of the week?



             Abstract

             Scheduling eccentric-based injury prevention programs (IPP) during the common 6-day
             micro-cycle in Soccer is challenged by recovery and tapering phases. This study profiled
             muscle damage, neuromuscular performance, and perceptual responses to a lower-limb
             eccentric-based IPP administered 1 (MD+1) versus 3 days (MD+3) post-match. 18 semi-
             professional players were monitored daily during 3 in-season 6-day micro-cycles, including
             weekly competitive fixtures. Capillary creatine kinase concentration (CK), posterior lower
             limb isometric peak force (PF), counter-movement jump (CMJ) performance, and muscle
             soreness were assessed 24 h prior to match-day (baseline), and every 24 h up to 120 h
             post-match. The IPP consisted of lunges, single stiff leg dead-lifts, single leg-squats and
             Nordic hamstring exercises. Performing the IPP on MD+1 attenuated the decline in CK
             normally observed following match-play           (CON: 142%; MD+3: 166%; small
             differences). When IPP was delivered on MD+3, CK was higher versus CON and MD+1
             trials on both MD+4 (MD+3: 260%; CON: 146%; MD+1: 151%; moderate differences) and
             MD+5 (MD+3: 209%; CON: 125%; MD+1: 127%; small differences). Soreness ratings were
             not exacerbated when the IPP was delivered on MD+1, but when prescribed on MD+3,
             hamstring soreness ratings remained higher on MD+4 and MD+5 (small differences). No
             between trial differences were observed for PF and CMJ. Administering the IPP in the
             middle of the micro-cycle (MD+3) increased measures of muscle damage and soreness,
             which remained elevated on the day prior to the next match (MD+5). Accordingly, IPP
             should be scheduled early in the micro-cycle, to avoid compromising preparation for the
             following match.



             Keywords: injury prevention, scheduling, muscle, soccer



             Introduction

             Soccer has a problem with injuries. Injury rates in both professional 1-3 and amateur soccer
             (9.6 injuries/1000h 1) exceed those observed both in industrial occupational settings 4 and
             other outdoor sports 5. The economic burden of injuries is substantial 6, and has also been
             shown to transcend to soccer performance outcomes, where teams with more injuries have
             been less successful on the pitch 7,8. Whilst some soccer injuries are inevitable (i.e. trauma
             injuries), 58% of injuries occur without contact and are considered preventable 3. The most
             common injury type are muscle strain injuries (31-37%), predominantly occurring in the
             hamstrings, adductors, quadriceps and calves 1-3. Although injury prevention programs (IPP)
             are commonplace in high-level professional soccer teams, there is a lack of information

             A survey of 44 ‘Premier League’ teams from around the world identified that the adoption of
             IPP was ubiquitous, with an average of 5.1 ± 2.4 practitioners (doctors, physiotherapists,
             sport scientists) employed to administer the programs 9. Eccentric exercises were ranked
             the most effective modality implemented within IPP 9. The theoretical basis for the inclusion
             of eccentric strengthening exercises include the greater mechanical tension and strain
             exerted upon the muscle fibers 10, yielding increases in muscle fascicle length 11,12 that
             consequently increase muscle shortening velocity and force production at longer muscle
             lengths 10,12. Whilst IPP consisting of eccentric exercises are warranted on the basis of the
             enhanced muscle function and architectural adaptations, the residual muscle fatigue and
             damage incurred 13 presents a scheduling dilemma for injury prevention specialists. This
             challenge is exacerbated in soccer, where competition schedules mandate a delicate
             balance between providing adequate recovery from competition and training, in combination
             with a suitable maintenance stimulus to prevent declines in muscle strength and lower limb
             power that have been documented over the course of a season 14-16.



             According to the available literature, intense soccer training is not scheduled in the 24-48 h
             period post-match 17-19, to facilitate recovery of muscle function and damage. In micro-
             cycles consisting of one competitive match per week, the greatest volume of on-field training
             is typically scheduled in the middle of the training week, between 2-4 days prior to the match
             19,20
                  , with IPP most commonly delivered 48-72 h post-match 9. However, considering the
             muscle damage and residual fatigue inflicted from eccentric exercise may persist for 48-72
             hours 21-23, current IPP scheduling in the middle of the training week may impact upon
             subsequent physical match performance. Moreover, during congested fixture periods (2 or
             more matches per week) common to soccer, IPP are often sacrificed to prepare for, or
             compete in, the following match 9, which over-time may result in muscle de-training 14,15,24
             and render the player more susceptible to injury 25. To our knowledge, a dearth of evidence
             is available regarding the scheduling and subsequent recovery from an IPP session in
             relation to soccer matches 9.



             The purpose of this study was to examine the acute impact of scheduling an eccentric-based
             lower-limb IPP on different days of the micro-cycle upon muscle function, damage, and
             soreness. Assessment of these muscle responses can inform the scheduling of IPP in
             soccer micro-cycles, and provide relevant insight to practitioners dealing with congested
             fixtures.

              Materials and methods

             Participants




Accepted Article
             Eighteen semi-professional outfield players (Age: 22.9 ± 4.5; Stature: 178.4 ± 8.7 cm; Body
             Mass: 74.5 ± 11.3 kg) were recruited from three teams competing in the 3rd and 4th tiers of
             the Australian Soccer pyramid during the 2015 season. These players typically undertake 2
             field-based training sessions, perform in one or two competitive fixtures, and 1-3 gymnasium
             conditioning sessions (on an independent, self-selected basis) per in-season week. The
             study obtained ethical approval from the Western Sydney University human research
             committee, and each player provided written informed consent to participate.



             Experimental Design

             Within a cross-over design, players were randomized into three groups within each team
             (n=6) to ensure that the order of experimental trials could be counter-balanced and limit the
             impact of extraneous factors such as weather conditions, training and competition loads etc.
             Allocation was performed using a spreadsheet to reduce between group differences in
             controlled trials (Hopkins, 2010), using participant characteristics in the following priority
             order: team, peak posterior limb isometric force (see details below), positional role, age and
             body mass. Table 1 displays the characteristics of players in each group



             Over a 3-week period, players undertook three experimental conditions in 6-day micro-
             cycles. The micro-cycles were selected on the basis that only one match was scheduled on
             weekends, and there were no expected changes to the routine training program that
             included two soccer training sessions each week. The 6-day micro-cycles commenced on
             match-day (MD), and outcome measures were tracked for the following 5-days, which
             included on-field training sessions scheduled 3 (MD+3) and 5 days (MD+5) post MD. During
             each micro-cycle, players training and match training loads were determined; and subjective,
             biochemical and performance recovery profiles were assessed 24 h prior to match-day
             (baseline), and 24 (MD+1), 48 (MD+2), 72 (MD+3), 96 (MD+4) and 120 h (MD+5) post-
             match.



             The experimental design included a control micro-cycle (CON), in which the players training
             loads and recovery parameters were monitored without any intervention. The impact of
             scheduling was examined using two treatment trials in which an eccentric-based IPP
             focusing on the anterior and posterior thigh muscles was administered either ~24- (MD+ 1)
             or ~72-h (MD+3) post-match, immediately following the recordings of muscle performance,
             damage and recovery measures. We selected the scheduling in our two treatment trials
             based on the survey of McCall and colleagues 9, which demonstrated that whilst the majority
             (61%) of teams prescribed IPP between 48-72 h post-match, a notable proportion (16%)
             delivered an IPP within 24 h of the match, highlighting the uncertainty in professional
             practice.

             limb) and Nordic hamstring exercises (NHE) performed on a Bosu-ball (4 x 5 repetitions).
             The Bosu-ball was used for the NHE to accentuate the eccentric stimulus at extended
             muscle lengths, the joint position which corresponds with the mechanism of hamstring injury

                and positioning in which the greatest NHE-induced strength gains are observed 12. These
             exercises were selected because injuries to the hamstring and quadriceps are amongst the
             most prevalent in soccer 1-3, and that eccentric exercises are considered the most important
             feature of IPP by soccer specialists 9. The IPP was performed under direct supervision of
             both a chartered physiotherapist (MW) and a sport scientist (RL) to ensure appropriate and
             consistent exercise techniques. Players had been familiarized with the IPP program
             following two training sessions in the 2-weeks preceding the study.



             Outcome Measures

             On the day prior to the match, and each day of the micro-cycle (excluding match-day),
             players attended a training ground to perform the battery of measures. Upon arrival, players
             warmed-up by running around a marked area on the training pitch for 5-minutes at 10 km/h
             (running speed standardized via a metronome). Upon completion, a capillary blood sample
             was drawn to determine plasma creatine kinase, which was used as an indirect estimate of
             muscle damage 27. Next, players were fitted with a knee brace to undertake the assessment
             of posterior lower-limb isometric peak force. During a subsequent 4-min rest interval players
             recorded their subjective evaluations of any training load incurred over the previous 24
             hours, and ratings of perceived muscle soreness. Finally, players performed the maximal
             counter-movement jump assessments. Players were familiarized with the outcome measure
             procedures on two occasions prior to data collection.



             Creatine Kinase

             Duplicate capillary blood samples were drawn from the fingertip and collected in heparinzed
             capillary tubes. 30 μl samples were immediately transferred onto reagent strips and the
             concentration of creatine kinase in the plasma was measured via Reflectance photometry
             (Reflotron IV, Boehringer Mannheim, Germany). The spectrometer was calibrated prior to
             each day using manufacturer supplied calibration strips. Where duplicate samples were
             either dubious or markedly different, additional samples were collected. The mean of two
             acceptable CK recordings was used for subsequent analysis (3.5% coefficient of variation;
             measurement range: 24.4-1400 UL-1).



             Isometric Muscle Strength

             Posterior lower limb isometric peak force was measured on the dominant limb at 30° of knee
             flexion (0° = full knee extension) according to the methods adopted in previous soccer
             studies 21,28. We adopted an isometric modality that is sensitive to neuromuscular fatigue

              induced by soccer match-play 21,28, and deemed feasible for daily monitoring to limit the
             impact of the maximum contractions upon the time-course of muscle function recovery.
             Knee flexion angle was sustained throughout the contraction using a knee brace that was

             fixed according to an inherent goniometer (Orthopaedic Appliances Pty Ltd, Australia). The
             heel of the dominant leg was placed on a 1000hz piezoelectric force platform (Kistler
             Instruments Pty Ltd, Australia) wired to a data acquisition system and attached to a plinth,
             with the non-dominant leg fully extended below the plinth (See Figure 2). Players were
             instructed to push their dominant heel into the force platform “as fast and as forcefully as
             possible” during three maximal 3 s contractions, separated by a 2-min rest period. Force
             data was smoothed with a sliding 200 ms window and the peak force (N) was recorded for
             analysis, having corrected for passive limb-mass. The typical error (expressed as a
             percentage co-efficient of variation) established from the three baseline (MD-1) recordings of
             isometric peak force was 8.2 % (90% confidence intervals [CI]: 6.7 to 11.2%).



             Counter-movement Jump

             The counter-movement jump is a commonly used tool to track neuromuscular recovery
             following soccer match-play 21,29. Players performed two maximal counter-movement jumps
             (CMJ; hands placed on hips for the duration of the attempt), interceded by 2 minutes of
             passive recovery. The speed and depth of the countermovement phase were self-selected.
             Players performed the CMJ on a force platform (Precision Calibration Systems, Sydney,
             Australia), with force signal sampled at 1000Hz. The analogue to digital converter signal
             was calibrated prior to each day using a known mass, and the signal was zeroed in between
             each participant to avoid drift. The vertical force trace was collected (Powerlab 16/35, ADI
             instruments, Australia; 16-bit analogue to digital conversion) and smoothed by a digital low
             pass filter cut off at 50 Hz. The flight-time:contraction-time ratio was recorded according to
             previously outlined procedures 30, and the jump height (cm) estimated from time in flight 31.
             The baseline coefficients of variation for CMJ height and flight-time:contraction-time ratio
             were 5.8% (CI: 4.8-7.9%) and 9.5% (CI: 7.7-12.7%), respectively.



             Perceived Muscle Soreness

             Daily ratings of perceived soreness in the hamstring and quadricep muscle groups were
             reported at rest. Players used a 100 mm visual analogue scale superimposed with the
             following verbal anchors: 0 = “absolutely no soreness”, and 100 = “the most muscle
             soreness that they could possibly bear” 32.

              Monitoring Variables

             External Load




Accepted Article
             During matches, players wore a 10Hz GPS device (MinimaX S4, Catapult, Australia) affixed
             in a neoprene under-garment worn beneath their training/playing jersey. Players wore the
             same device and undergarment throughout the study to attenuate within-subject error.
             Doppler velocity data was pre-processed using the manufacturers ‘Intelligent Motion Filter’
             and the minimum effort duration was set at 0.2 secs (Catapult Sprint, version 5.1.7, Catapult
             Sports, Australia). GPS data were extracted and further processed using R (version 3.01).
             Instantaneous observations of velocity and acceleration were discarded when the number of
             satellites informing the receiver was less than 6, and/or the horizontal dilution of precision
             (HDOP) was less than 1.25. The average proportion of data discarded during match files
             was 0.19 ± 0.21% of total playing time. All match observations therefore met the inclusion
             criteria, whereby extracted instantaneous data accounted for <3% of the total session
             duration. Players’ total distance covered (TDC) and that covered at high- (HSR; > 15.0 kmh-
             1
              ) and sprinting (SPR; > 23.0 kmh-1) running speeds were computed for each session.



             Internal Load

             The internal load was calculated using the session-RPE method 33, recorded 10 minutes
             after all training and matches during each micro-cycle. Players were also asked to
             retrospectively rate exertion and provide training duration(s) for any additional conditioning
             sessions performed outside of the team environment. These ratings were collected on a
             daily basis during the recovery profiling assessments for the previous 24-hour period.
             Recent observations suggest that sessional RPE ratings are robust measures even when
             collected retrospectively 34.



             Statistics

             For statistical analysis, outcome measures were expressed as change scores from the
             relevant micro-cycle baseline measure, and subsequently log-transformed to reduce non-
             uniformity error. Linear mixed models (IBM SPSS version 23.0, Armonk, NY) were used to
             examine the impact of scheduling upon the recovery time-course of muscle function,
             soreness and damage markers. The experimental trial and measurement day were entered
             into the model as fixed factors, and within-player variance was modeled as a random factor.
             In addition, sRPE and baseline measures of the relevant dependent variable were imputed
             as covariates in the model. Baseline recordings accounted for week-to-week changes, and
             sRPE adjusted for variations in internal training load both within and between micro-cycles
             for each individual player. P-values generated from least-squared difference post hoc tests,
             in combination with back-transformed estimated marginal mean effect statistics, were
             imputed into a spreadsheet 35 to derive magnitude-based inferences. The magnitude of the
             effect was classified as small, moderate, or large according to standardized fractions (0.2,
             0.6, and 1.2) of the pooled between-subject standard deviation, calculated from measures
             collected 24 h post-match (MD+1) in the each trial. We elected to use MD+1 data to anchor
             standardized thresholds considering the large between-subject variation in responses to

             Results

             one micro-cycle, before withdrawing due to a contact injury sustained during a match.

             Discussion

             In this study we examined the impact of IPP scheduling within 6-day micro-cycles upon
             muscle function, soreness, and creatine kinase as an indirect measure of damage.
             Administering the eccentric-based IPP 24 hours following matches slowed the rate of
             creatine kinase decay, but did not exacerbate soreness beyond the typical recovery time-
             course. In contrast, delivering the IPP in the middle of the micro-cycle (MD+3) increased
             measures of soreness and damage, which remained elevated on the day prior to the
             following match (MD+5). IPP scheduling had no impact upon the muscle function measures
             adopted in this study. To our knowledge, this is the first study to examine the impact of IPP
             scheduling during a typical micro-cycle in soccer, and our preliminary findings infer that
             administering eccentric-based exercises in the middle of the training week may negatively
             impact upon preparation for the following match. Moreover, delivery early in the micro-cycle
             ensures that the training stimulus is not sacrificed during congested fixtures periods in which
             matches are played every 3-4 days.



             Surveys of current industry practice suggest that IPP are commonly scheduled 48-72 hours
             following a match, and that eccentric-based exercises are considered the most effective
             modality 9. When we administered an eccentric-based IPP 72 hours following match-play

             higher residual values of CK prior to team-sport training and competitive matches have been
             associated with reduced explosive running 37 and technical performance ratings 38.
             Whereas, self-reported muscle soreness collected pre-training or pre-match have a trivial
             association with external load parameters 39,40, and to the authors knowledge there is no
             published literature evaluating the impact of soreness ratings on subsequent non-contact
             injury risk. Notwithstanding, collectively these observations would suggest that scheduling
             IPP in the middle of the micro-cycle may compromise performance in the following match,
             however further work may be necessary to confirm whether repeated high-intensity actions
             that better reflect the nature of soccer activity are unhindered following eccentric IPP.



             Although training load studies have implied that the greatest volume of both on-field 19,20 and
             IPP training 9 is performed in the middle of the micro-cycle, following approximately 24-48 h
             post-match recovery 17-19, 7 of the 44 teams surveyed by McCall and colleagues 9 reported
             delivering an IPP within 24 h post-match. When IPP was scheduled on MD+1 in the current
             study, CK decay was slowed 48 h post-match, but returned to baseline after 72 h, and the
             time-course of muscle function and soreness recovery post-match was not affected. These
             observations to some degree are supported by previous work, which showed that
             prescribing an upper-body strength training session 24 h following a bout of damaging lower-
             limb eccentric actions 13 did not adversely impact recovery kinetics (hamstring strength, CK,
             muscle soreness).        Whilst training structures in micro-cycles consisting of weekly
             competition schedules typically comprise of recovery and regenerative strategies, the
             inclusion of additional training 24 h post-match may optimize the limited time available for
             training, and offset the seasonal losses in strength and power in team-sports 14-16. Whilst a
             potentially attractive solution to training prescription in congested competition schedules,
             further work is necessary to determine both the acute and chronic responses to
             administering an IPP during the typical muscle regenerative phase of the weekly soccer
             micro-cycle in which muscle function may be compromised.



             The increase in creatine kinase observed 24 h post match in this study (256% vs. 98-300%),
             together with the decay recorded at 48 (142% vs. 45-300%) and 72 h (138% vs. 90-202%) in
             the control trial, was comparable to previous research 21-23,41. Furthermore, the response
             magnitudes for soreness recorded in our control trial far exceeded those reported previously
             in elite cohorts 21,22,42 at 24 and 48 h post-match. Despite the robust CK and soreness
             responses observed, the muscle function measures adopted in our study were generally not
             sensitive to soccer match-play. Only peak counter-movement jump height was reduced 24
             hours post-match, with no change documented in FT:CT ratio, or the isometric assessment
             of posterior lower-limb peak force. Our data on lower-limb power and strength are in

             following team-sports match play 21,29. Given the equivalent internal responses to soccer
             match-play we observed when contrasting to previous work, it is difficult to reconcile this

             players were at times selected as substitutes or were early withdrawals from the game,

             Of note was that the IPP induced the same acute CK magnitude response versus match-
             play, when delivered on MD+3. This was surprising considering that the players were
             familiar with the IPP, but may reflect the lower training status of our semi-professional
             cohort. For example, the mean baseline isometric peak strength recorded in this study was
             ~20-30% lower than that reported for the same procedure in professional players 21,28. It is
             also noteworthy that individuals with a strength training history recover muscle function and
             CK responses back to baseline quicker than their untrained counterparts 43. It may be the
             case that professional players routinely exposed to eccentric muscle actions during both IPP
             and soccer activity have a blunted response and faster CK decay following IPP. This may
             be due to structural reinforcement of muscle fibers, or the addition of sarcomeres in series
             which renders the fascicles more resistant to stretch, potentially reducing mechanical
             disruption and microscopic trauma 44. The semi-professional cohort examined in this study
             had a mixed strength-training history, but were familiar with lower-limb eccentric exercises,
             and were exposed to the eccentric nature of soccer activity between 3-4 times per week,
             with a particularly rigorous soreness and CK response to matches. Hence, whilst
             generalization of the current findings to professional programs is speculative, we would
             caution against administering eccentric-based IPP in the middle of the micro-cycle in
             professional team-sports.



             The major limiting factor of the current study was the administration of a standardized IPP
             that did not take into consideration the differing training histories and capacities of the
             individual players. We recognize that in applied practice athletes may undertake tailored
             IPP, but we considered standardization necessary given the cross-over design adopted, and
             the challenges in prescribing individualized eccentric training intensity and volume. In
             contrast, we were unable to standardize the match stimulus given our preference for an
             ecologically natured study, and with the exception of load monitoring could not access the
             players on match-day to ascertain measures of muscle function, damage and soreness
             immediately pre- and post matches. An examination of physical match performance
             following the IPP delivery at MD+1 or MD+3 may have provided further insight on the impact
             of IPP scheduling, however we omitted this analysis considering the high-degree of
             between-match variation in high-speed running and sprinting 45. Interpretation of CK derived
             from blood samples as an indicator of muscle damage is confounded by its unknown origin,
             and can often be explained by blunt force traumas in sporting settings where collisions are
             commonplace 46. Finally, generalizability of the current findings should be tempered
             considering the semi-professional cohort adopted, whose training history, micro-cycle
             schedules, and capacity may influence the acute muscle responses following the eccentric-
             IPP, and may not directly translate into professional practice.

             Perspectives

             The incidence and location of injuries in Soccer is well established 1-3, and substantial
             resources have been allocated to injury prevention 9. However, scheduling of eccentric-
             based injury prevention programs is challenged by fixture congestion, and the inherent need
             to recover from, and prepare for, competitive matches. The insights from this study provide
             some preliminary evidence to guide sports medicine professional practice, however further

Capillary creatine kinase, isometric posterior lower-limb peak force, countermovement jump and hamstring and quadriceps soreness were measured from baseline to 120 h after match. Linear mixed models were used with magnitude-based inferences.",
   "findings": "Creatine kinase was 142% of baseline at MD+2 in control, 197% after MD+1 and 166% after MD+3. On MD+4, creatine kinase was 260% after MD+3 versus 146% in control and 151% after MD+1, and on MD+5 it was 209% versus 125% and 127%. Peak force, flight time to contraction time ratio and countermovement jump did not differ between trials.",
   "limitations": "The sample was small (18 players, 17 complete) and drawn from one season of semi-professional players in tiers 3 and 4, with sex not stated. The program was standardized and not tailored to each player. Match loads were lower on the MD+3 match (total distance 6839 m versus 7900 m on MD+1 and 8500 m in control), and the authors note that the match stimulus was not controlled. Creatine kinase has an unknown origin in sport, and the performance measures were not sensitive to match play.",
   "practicalImplications": "In a one-match weekly microcycle, eccentric injury prevention work given 3 days after a match left creatine kinase and hamstring soreness elevated on the day before the next match. Given 1 day after the match, it did not add to soreness or delay the return of creatine kinase toward baseline. Schedule choice should be checked against each player's soreness and creatine kinase responses.",
   "athleteDev": "For a weekly microcycle with one match, this study suggests placing eccentric injury prevention work about 24 h after the match rather than around 72 h, since the later timing kept soreness and creatine kinase raised before the next match.    "rtp": "This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It included only uninjured players, and it measured creatine kinase, soreness and performance responses to a standard program rather than injury outcomes or rehabilitation progress."

211	                           The surgery was performed under general anesthesia, with the patient placed in the
212	                      prone position, and without the usage of a tourniquet. A longitudinal incision was made
213	                      at the border of the proximal to the middle third of the thigh with a sharp dissection of
214	                      the fascia. After longitudinally incising the fascia, we found extensive scar formation
215	                      around the sciatic nerve starting at the long head of the biceps femoris, as described in the
216	                      MRI, with nerve compression (Figure 1a,b). The nerve was primarily dissected distally
217	                      around the healthy tissue before we performed microscopic neurolysis from distal to
218	                      proximal. We did not re-attach the long head of the biceps femoris due to the vital origins
219	                      of the semimembranosus and semitendinosus and the retraction of the biceps femoris as
220	                      a consequence of the chronicity of the injury. No drainage equipment was applied after
221	                      the surgery due to exact coagulation. Postoperatively, a splint was not applied, nor was an
222	                      orthosis administered, and the patient’s right lower limb was immediately immobilized.
223	                      Four weeks postoperatively, the patient reported ameliorated pain and the giving way
224	                      phenomenon. Furthermore, he began to engage in mild sports activity and was able to
225	                      return to sports several weeks later. Two years following the operation, the patient is still
226	                      free of complaints, and his sports level has returned to that before his injury.

228	                      3. Case Report Two
229	                           Next, we present the case of a 49-year-old male patient who slipped and fell at home
230	                      and felt immediate pain in his left buttock. He was transferred to a local hospital and was
231	                      diagnosed with a left hip contusion after obtaining an X-ray. Due to prolonged pain and
232	                      a distinct hematoma, he visited another hospital two weeks later. He was admitted to an
233	                      MRI, through which a complete tear of the proximal hamstring tendons with a retraction of
234	                      over 10 cm was diagnosed. Nevertheless, the patient was not admitted to surgery and was
235	                      treated conservatively with rest, ice, compression, and elevation (RICE); physical therapy;
236	                      and stationary rehab. Two years later, the patient presented with persistent posterior thigh
237	                      pain, a strength deficit, pain while sitting, paresthesia throughout the lateral part of the
238	                      leg and the dorsum of the foot and a giving way phenomenon due to shooting pain in
239	                      the left buttock. An electromyographic study of the anterior tibialis muscle and a nerve
240	                      conduction study of the tibial nerve showed normal nerve and muscle function compared
241	                      to the right leg.
242	                           A recent MRI showed fatty degeneration of the hamstring muscle group and scar
243	                      formation around the sciatic nerve (Figure 2a). Despite the availability of physiological
244	                      nerve conduction studies, we opted for open neurolysis of the sciatic nerve since the patient
245	                      presented persistent symptoms over a period of two years despite undergoing prolonged
246	                      physical therapy. As in the first case, we chose to make a longitudinal incision with the
247	                      patient lying in the prone position, for which a tourniquet was not used. After the dissection
248	                      and incision of the fascia, the sciatic nerve was visualized and found to be stretched due
249	                      to scar formation caused by the former peritendineum around the nerve, as shown in
250	                      Figure 2b. Microscopic neurolysis was performed, and in this case, we reattached the
251	                      biceps femoris muscle to the semimembranosus to place an additional layer over the nerve
252	                      before closing the fascia to prevent further scar formation. We also chose to administer
253	                      functional rehabilitation without a splint or orthosis, and physical therapy was started
254	                      immediately after the surgery. Postoperatively, the giving way phenomenon and shooting
255	                      pain disappeared over weeks, whereas the strength deficit, paresthesia, and posterior thigh
256	                      pain while sitting persisted for as long as one year postoperatively.

475	                                   be performed accurately in cases of vague posterior thigh pain. The need for an MRI
476	                                   should be generously interpreted for all patients presenting with persistent posterior thigh
477	                                   pain [9,10]. Proximal hamstring injuries can be classified into acute or chronic proximal
478	                                   hamstring tears depending on the time of diagnosis, which is often delayed because of late
479	                                   consultation or a missed diagnosis. There is still no consensus about the definition of an
480	                                   acute injury. A proposed timeframe of under six weeks has yet to be widely accepted [11].
481	                                   Wood et al. defined an MRI-based classification of a proximal hamstring tear in 2012
482	                                   (Table 1), including therapy recommendations depending on the number of ruptured
483	                                   tendons and the grade of muscle retraction [12]. Surgical treatment is never recommended
484	                                   for simple muscle strains at the musculotendinous unit classified as a Type-Two injury.
485	                                   Surgery is recommended in cases of bony avulsions, which are primarily obtained in
486	                                   adolescents (Type-One injury); incomplete tears (Type-Three injuries), when the patient is
487	                                   still symptomatic after conservative treatment; or Type-Three injuries when the tendons
488	                                   are retracted over 2 cm. Complete tears are classified as Type-Four or Type-Five injuries,
489	                                   depending on the grade of retraction. Nevertheless, surgery is obligatory for all patients
490	                                   with complete hamstring tears. The presence of sciatic nerve symptoms is not included in
491	                                   this classification [12].
